Movable Type

What the press actually changed

Cities that got a press grew faster. Everything about why is still argued.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected 2 timesUpdated 21 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedCorrectedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

Gutenberg's press is the standard example of technology changing history, which is exactly why the historians who study it spend most of their time disagreeing about what it changed.

If you keep one line

The machine makes cheap copies; institutions make them trustworthy. Never confuse the two.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

The mechanics arrived around 1450 in Mainz: movable metal type, an oil-based ink that would stick to it, and a screw press adapted from wine-making. By 1500, by Fernand Braudel's count, presses were operating in some 236 European towns. That uneven adoption is what makes the period tractable, because it gives you something rare in history — a natural experiment.

Jeremiah Dittmar used it. Cities that adopted the press between 1450 and 1500 grew faster over the following century than comparable cities that didn't, with no growth advantage beforehand. His difference-in-differences estimate puts the gap at more than 30 percentage points of population growth from 1500 to 1600, in a century when the average city grew by roughly 30 per cent. Instrumenting adoption with distance from Mainz — presses spread outward from where the technology was — pushes the estimate higher still.

Elizabeth Eisenstein's argument is the classic one: print produced 'fixity'. Once a text could be reproduced identically thousands of times, errors stopped accumulating with each copy, results could be compared across distance, and standardised diagrams and tables became possible — which is a precondition for cumulative science rather than a consequence of it.

Adrian Johns wrote the strongest rebuttal. Early print was chaotic: piracy, unauthorised editions, garbled reprints and outright forgery were endemic, and readers had no reason to trust a printed book more than a manuscript. Fixity, he argues, was not a property of the press but an achievement — built slowly through guilds, licensing, reputational policing and law. If he's right, the causal arrow runs through institutions, and the machine was necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

01By the numbers

236European towns with a printing press by 1500, the end of the incunabula period: Fernand Braudel's count, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Global spread of the printing press'
>30 ppExtra population growth, 1500–1600, for cities that adopted the press early, against average city growth of 0.27 log points: Jeremiah Dittmar, 'Information Technology and Economic Change: The Impact of the Printing Press', Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(3), 2011 (read in the January 2011 working paper)
1998Johns publishes the rebuttal that split the field: Adrian Johns, 'The Nature of the Book', University of Chicago Press, 1998 (Internet Archive catalogue record)

02How it happened

  1. ~1450Gutenberg assembles movable metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press in Mainz.
  2. 1455The 42-line Bible demonstrates the output can match manuscript quality at scale.
  3. 1500Presses are operating in some 236 European towns, by Braudel's count.
  4. 1517Luther's theses spread at a speed the church's enforcement machinery cannot match.
  5. 1979Eisenstein publishes 'The Printing Press as an Agent of Change' and defines the field.
  6. 1998Adrian Johns publishes 'The Nature of the Book' and argues fixity was made, not given.

03Who did the work

Johannes GutenbergCombined four existing technologies into one system and died in relative obscurity after losing the lawsuit.
Elizabeth EisensteinMade the case that print's standardising effect was a precondition for modern science.
Adrian JohnsArgued print's reliability was a social achievement, not a mechanical property — the sharpest counterargument in the field.

04Where it is contested

Dittmar's instrument — distance from Mainz — is doing a lot of work, and distance from Mainz correlates with plenty of other things, including trade routes and proximity to the commercial core of Europe. The correlation between presses and growth is robust; the causal identification is the part specialists argue over.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 10 · Sept 2026 · Angicos and the printing press.

The Banking Model of Education said Freire's workers at Angicos learned to read in forty-five days, and printed 45 days as a figure. The Paulo Freire Institute's own chronology has the lessons running from late January to early April 1963; the programme was named for its forty hours of instruction, after which 300 of the 380 who began were certified literate. The entry now says forty hours. Movable Type said Jeremiah Dittmar's estimate put the growth advantage of early-printing cities at 35 percentage points or more. The paper says over 30, and 35 appears nowhere in it. Both figures had been printed under the promise that they were sourced; neither line named where it came from, and both now do.

№ 14 · Sept 2026 · Three figures in the Press.

Movable Type said presses were operating in about 205 European cities by 1500, out of more than a thousand. Neither number is in the paper the entry relies on; Fernand Braudel's count, the one found, is 236 towns, and the entry now gives his. Cost Disease said New York subway construction runs about $1.5 billion a kilometre. The Transit Costs Project's own New York study puts Phase 1 of the Second Avenue Subway at about $1.7 billion a kilometre, and the entry now says so. In Defense of Bubbles said 85 to 95 per cent of the fibre laid in the 1990s sat dark after the bust. Every account found attributes the range to unnamed analysts, and no study behind it could be opened, so the number is gone.

06What I changed my mind about

I used to treat 'the printing press caused the scientific revolution' as settled background. Johns' argument reframed it: the machine made cheap copies, and the trustworthiness of those copies had to be built afterwards by boring institutional work. That's the same pattern as the internet, which is why it stopped feeling like history.
